b: It’s four answers to four questions. Here we go…
1. My coworker agrees with everything no matter what
I have a coworker who will say they agree with everything, even if the conversation started out with them saying something you disagreed with. For example:

Coworker: Hey, can I get your input on this issue? I think we should go with X.
Me: I see why you suggest X but I think that is a bad solution and think Y is a better solution.
Coworker: Yes, that’s exactly what I was thinking — agreed.

Me: I think the process we have for X isn’t great. Can we change it?
Coworker: Hm, okay, I found this process doc we have for it and added your requested change. Can you look it over?
Me: I read the whole thing, and my suggestion is actually contradicting all other info in the document. Stick to what it says in the document– it already addresses the issue I’m having. It seems like the issue is that we need to recirculate this document and remind people we already have this process.
Coworker: EXACTLY.

Why would you suggest X if you were also thinking Y? Why did you make the changes I requested if you agree they contradict all the other info?! It happens ALL THE TIME and the worst part is that it doesn’t seem like anyone notices but me! I find it so grating because I think it’s a way to hide his lack of expertise and a way of taking other people’s ideas and pretending like he was the one who introduced them in the first place.
Am I being overly sensitive here? Should I just chalk it up to a funny quirk my coworker has that I just need to get used to? Or is this truly as bananapants and manipulative as I feel it is?
No, this is genuinely aggravating and makes your coworker look incompetent; it’s not a funny quirk.

I suspect what’s behind it is insecurity; they don’t feel confident in their own judgment and expertise, and they’re trying to cover that up (both by taking every suggestion you make and by pretending they didn’t just suggest something else).
In your first example, it might make sense to dig into it by saying something like, “Well, wait — you were just suggesting X, so if you think that’s a better way to go, we should talk that through.”

In the second example, you could maybe say, “Wait, did I miss something? You had added my change in; I’m saying it doesn’t seem like it belongs there, but what’s your thinking on the whole thing?” … and then maybe, “I don’t want you to feel like you have to implement whatever I suggest; if my suggestion doesn’t seem right to you, please push back.”

But ultimately it’s probably a conversation to have with their manager if this keeps happening; their manager is better positioned to dig into what’s going on and why (and if nothing else, should be aware that this person’s judgment seems to be off).

For whatever reason, it’s become common at my office for people to whisper when they want to have a clandestine conversation. Whispering drives me nuts. Theoretically it would be possible for the offending parties to simply go into an empty office and close the door. In practice, the whispering simply happens in the hallway.

Obviously I want to know the content of the whispers, but that’s never going to happen. I do want the distracting behavior to stop. Do I have standing to raise this with the whispering parties? Or do I leave it alone? For context, the offenders are generally management. I am very much not management, but I’ve been working here for years.

It’s normal to find whispering more distracting than normal-level conversation would be; your brain is used to tuning out conversation around you while you work, but whispering catches your ears in a different way and can be harder to block out (perhaps in part because your brain knows people are specifically trying not to be heard and it can stir up anxiety or concern).

If these were peers or people junior to you, you’d be able to say, “I’m finding the whispering so distracting — would you mind moving somewhere else if you need privacy?” But since they’re management and you’re “very much not,” you don’t really have the standing to say that. At most, you could mention to your boss that it’s happening a lot and making it hard to focus, and she might speak to them on your behalf. Otherwise, though: headphones.

I was diagnosed with autism at the beginning of this year and it’s helped me understand a lot of things I’ve been struggling with for years, including the fact that I find working in-person extremely difficult — turns out I find it exhausting due to masking! Fortunately I’m a programmer and can do my work 100% remotely, and my last two jobs were remote. When I started at this job, I averaged two days a week in the office, and that was manageable for me. Unfortunately, my employer decided to go from hybrid to 100% in-person and my workplace is basically the least sensory-friendly place on earth: all open office (only the CEO has a private office — even HR just has a conference room they take turns using), not even cubicles, just rows of desks. And we’re chronically short of conference rooms so people often take meetings from their desks.

My department revolted and was grudgingly allowed one work-from-home day a week. I gave it a solid try for two months and it simply did not work for me. I was too tired to do anything except work. I didn’t have enough energy to do normal things like buy groceries, clean, or play with my dog. So I asked about getting an accommodation. My psychiatrist told them I needed to work from home at least three days a week and suggested various other things they could do (a private office, a quieter workspace, etc).

My workplace sat on this request for over a month and then grudgingly allowed me a second work-from-home day per week, suggested I try noise-cancelling headphones (which I’d already been using for years), and implemented none of the other suggestions. I’ve been trying this accommodation for the last several months and it’s better than being in office four days a week but it’s not enough. I’m still struggling a lot, to the point that it’s not viable in the long-term.

My understanding of ADA accommodations is that it’s meant to be an interactive process and I should be able to go back to HR, tell them the current situation is not sufficient, and ask for further accommodations, but I’m afraid to do that because I’m already in hot water at work a little. Unfortunately it’s been a pretty bad year for me personally, so I had to take several weeks off for family emergencies. We theoretically have unlimited PTO, but my manager took me aside and said that his superiors felt I’d taken too much time off this year and I needed to be careful about taking more. I also got a lower rating than usual on my most recent review, although no specific reason was cited for it and it wasn’t low enough to get put on a PIP.

I think in the long-term I just need to find a 100% remote job, but in the current tech job market that could take a year or more, and applying and interviewing burn energy I just don’t have. So I guess my two real questions are: from an ADA perspective, should my job be expected to revisit and offer further accommodations since the ones they initially offered are insufficient? And, in the real world, is this something it actually makes sense to try and pursue?

Legally, yes, ADA accommodations are supposed to be an interactive process, and if an accommodation isn’t working sufficiently well, you’re supposed to be able to go back to your employer and say, “This hasn’t solved the problem so can we talk about what else we can try?”

Realistically … it depends. In a context where your boss has already told you they think you’ve taken too much time off and you got a lower-than-normal rating on your review, there’s definitely a risk they’re not going to be amenable. (There would be that risk even without those circumstances, but those things aren’t strengthening your position.) In theory, those things shouldn’t be relevant at all — time off and working remotely are two different things, and the idea with an accommodation is that it’s supposed to help you do your job (so you should be able to argue that if your performance has suffered, it may be specifically because you’re working from home less than you were previously) — but in reality, it can affect how flexible they’re willing to be with you. Again, the law says it shouldn’t, but what the law requires and what happens in practice aren’t always the same thing.

That said, you’re struggling pretty significantly, so I’d say it makes sense to at least try and see what happens, ideally with new documentation from your doctor that specifically says the fewer-than-she-recommended days aren’t sufficient.

4. References when my boss is my husband
For 15 years, I’ve worked for a small family-owned company. We were up to 10 employees but are now down to two. We are preparing to close, so it’s time to start job hunting.

My problem is references. Two years ago, the boss (the other employee) and I got married … to each other. There’s no scandal, nothing to feel bad about. However, I obviously can’t use him as a work reference since we are married. So, what do I do for references? It’s been 15 years since I worked elsewhere. Those references are now old/dated/stale. I have two references from solid volunteer work I’ve done, but they’re not related to my field. I do have a customer who I’ve worked with a good deal. She’s seen and been the recipient of years of my good work. Would it be okay to have a customer, soon to be former customer, as a reference? What about my managers in the volunteer work? Finally, what about a manager from 15 years ago? Is it worthwhile to use him? Of course, I’d ask each of them for permission to use them as references, I’m just not sure who is/are my best options.

Be up-front with employers about the situation! “My husband owns the business, and I assume you don’t want him as a reference! I’m happy to put you in touch with customers I’ve worked closely with, managers from volunteer work, or a manager from my previous job, although that was 15 years ago. Who would you find most helpful?”
If you have to supply references before you have an opportunity to ask that, I’d list the ones above, and then just explain the context for them when you’re further along in the process.
